newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea issues veiled threat over nuclear accord.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea issues veiled threat over nuclear accord.

text.p: North Korea issued a veiled warning to the United States on Tuesday that their landmark 1994 nuclear agreement could be jeopardised by Washington's stand over a submarine incident.
The submarine landed 26 North Koreans on an east coast beach last month. Twenty-two have been killed and Pyongyang has threatened "merciless retaliation".
A Pyongyang foreign ministry spokesman, quoted by the Korean Central News Agency, took issue with comments made in Seoul last week by U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord.

Lord said Washington and Seoul would press ahead with the agreement under which Pyongyang pledged to freeze its nascent nuclear weapons programme in return for two nuclear reactors financed largely by South Korea.
However, without referring directly to the submarine incident, he told a news conference "there would be a pause in the pace of our activities".
Seoul has said it cannot send a site inspection team to North Korea to plan construction of the light water reactors until the team's safety can be guaranteed.

"The U.S. side confirmed it would continue with the provision of light-water reactors and at the same time expressed understanding of the 'stand' of the South Korean authorities to delay the provision on the pretext of the 'incident of the submarine'," KCNA said.
"If it is true it means that the United States intends to use 'the submarine incident' as a lever for pressure on us by directly linking it with the implementation of the (nuclear agreement)."

It warned Washington against "trying to use the incident for its sinister political purpose" and said that if provision of the reactors was left to Seoul it would "have a decisive influence on the implementation of the agreement".
"We have clarified more than once that if the implementation of the agreement is inconvenient and bothersome to the U.S. side, we have no intention to make a strong objection to its suspension."
The statement called for an official explanation from Washington on Lord's visit to South Korea.
Lord visited South Korea for three days in a display of solidarity with one of Washington's closest allies following the submarine intrusion.
At his news conference Lord called on North Korea to "change its attitude" to the South. The two Koreas have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean conflict.
